learn: A community is a place where people live, work and play.
A city is a big, busy community with tall buildings. A town is smaller.
A rural community is in the countryside, with farms and lots of open land.
check: A community in the countryside with farms is...
Which community has tall buildings and many people?
What do people do in a community?
lessons.try: Decide if you live in a city, a town or a rural community.

learn: Communities have places that help people.
A library lends books. A hospital helps sick people. A fire station holds fire trucks.
Parks give people space to play and rest.
check: Where do sick people get help?
lessons.try: Name three places in your community you have visited.

learn: People in communities work together to solve problems.
Neighbours may clean a park, help an older person or share food.
Volunteers help without being paid.
check: Do people in communities work together?
lessons.try: Think of one way your class could help your community.

learn: Rules are for a group, like a class or a family.
Laws are rules for everyone in a community, state or country.
Laws keep people safe and help things be fair.
check: To keep people safe and be fair
lessons.try: Name one law you know, like stopping at a red light.

learn: Speed limits tell drivers how fast they can go.
Seat belt laws keep people safe in cars.
Littering laws keep parks and streets clean.
check: What keeps people safe in cars?
lessons.try: Look for a traffic sign on your next walk or ride.

learn: Without rules, people could get hurt or be treated unfairly.
When we follow rules, everyone gets a fair turn.
If a rule is not fair, people can work together to change it peacefully.
check: How can people change an unfair rule?
lessons.try: Imagine a game with no rules. What would happen?

learn: A leader is someone who helps guide a group.
A principal leads a school. A coach leads a team.
Good leaders listen, are fair and help others.
lessons.try: Name a leader in your school.

learn: A mayor leads a city or town.
A governor leads a state.
The president leads the United States.
lessons.try: Find out the name of your town's mayor with a grown-up.

learn: In the United States, people choose many leaders by voting.
Each vote counts the same. The choice with the most votes wins.
Your class can vote too, like choosing a class pet name.
check: How do people choose many leaders?
The one with the most votes
Does each vote count the same?
lessons.try: Hold a vote at home about what to have for dinner.

learn: Maps have a title that tells what the map shows.
A map key or legend explains the symbols.
A compass rose shows the directions north, south, east and west.
check: What shows directions on a map?
lessons.try: Look at a map and find the title, key and compass rose.

learn: The four main directions are north, south, east and west.
On most maps, north is at the top and south is at the bottom.
East is on the right and west is on the left. Remember: Never Eat Soggy Waffles.
check: On most maps, north is at the...
lessons.try: Point north, south, east and west in your room.

learn: You can make a map of your school, house or neighbourhood.
Use symbols and make a key so others can read your map.
Add a compass rose so people know the directions.
check: What should your map have so others can read it?
What tells people the directions on your map?
lessons.try: Make a map of your street or block with a key.

learn: Landforms are shapes of land.
A mountain is very high land. A hill is lower. A valley is low land between hills.
A plain is wide, flat land. An island is land with water all around it.
check: Land with water all around it is...
lessons.try: Make a landform out of clay or play dough.

learn: Oceans are huge bodies of salt water.
Lakes have land all around them. Rivers flow across land to a lake or an ocean.
Most of Earth is covered by water.
check: Is most of Earth covered by water?
lessons.try: Find an ocean, a lake and a river on a map.

learn: Earth has seven continents: North America, South America, Europe, Asia, Africa, Australia and Antarctica.
Earth has five oceans: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic and Southern.
The United States is on the continent of North America.
lessons.try: Point to North America and the Pacific Ocean on a globe or world map.

learn: The past is what already happened. The present is now. The future is what will happen.
Words like yesterday, long ago and last year tell about the past.
Words like tomorrow and next year tell about the future.
lessons.try: Use "yesterday", "today" and "tomorrow" in sentences.

learn: A timeline shows events in the order they happened.
Older events go on the left. Newer events go on the right.
You can make a timeline of your own life.
check: Where do older events go on a timeline?
Can you make a timeline of your own life?
lessons.try: Make a timeline with three events from your life.

learn: Things change over time. Schools, toys and transportation are different from long ago.
Long ago, children wrote on small chalkboards called slates. Now we use paper and computers.
Some things stay the same: children still learn, play and help at home.
check: What did children write on long ago?
Do some things stay the same over time?
Transportation long ago and today is...
lessons.try: Ask an older person how school was different when they were young.

learn: Long ago, many families lived in small houses, cabins or farmhouses.
Homes were heated by fireplaces and wood stoves.
Water often came from a well or a pump, not a tap.
check: How were homes heated long ago?
Where did water often come from?
lessons.try: Draw a home from long ago and a home today.

learn: Families long ago grew much of their own food.
Children helped by fetching water, feeding animals and gathering eggs.
Clothes were washed by hand on a washboard.
check: What did children do long ago?
lessons.try: Name one chore you do and one chore children did long ago.

learn: Children played games like tag, hopscotch, marbles and jump rope.
Families told stories, sang songs and played music together.
Many of these games are still played today.
check: Which game was played long ago?
Are some old games still played?
lessons.try: Play a game of hopscotch or tag from long ago.

learn: Goods are things people make or grow that we can buy.
Apples, shoes and books are goods.
Producers make goods. Consumers buy and use them.
lessons.try: Name three goods in your kitchen.

learn: A service is work someone does for others.
A haircut, a bus ride and a doctor's check-up are services.
Teachers, nurses and mail carriers provide services.
check: Is a bus ride a good or a service?
lessons.try: Name a service your family uses.

learn: Long ago, people traded goods instead of using money. This is called barter.
A farmer might trade eggs for shoes.
Today we mostly use money, but you can still trade things with friends.
check: A farmer might trade eggs for...
What do we mostly use today?
lessons.try: Trade a sticker or a pencil with a family member.

learn: A penny is worth 1 cent. A nickel is worth 5 cents.
A dime is worth 10 cents, even though it is small. A quarter is worth 25 cents.
One hundred cents make one dollar.
check: How many cents make a dollar?
lessons.try: Sort real or play coins by their names.

learn: People earn money by working.
They spend money on needs first, like food and housing.
If there is money left, they may buy wants.
lessons.try: Make a list of needs and wants for a pretend shopping trip.

learn: Saving means keeping money to use later.
A bank keeps money safe. A piggy bank is a small home bank.
When you choose one thing, you give up another. Choosing wisely is important.
check: When you choose one thing you...
lessons.try: Pretend you have 10 dollars. Will you spend it all or save some?

learn: The American flag has 50 stars and 13 stripes. Its colours are red, white and blue.
The bald eagle is the national bird.
The Liberty Bell and the Statue of Liberty stand for freedom.
check: How many stripes are on the flag?
What do the Liberty Bell and the Statue of Liberty stand for?
lessons.try: Draw the flag and count the stripes as you draw.

learn: A monument is built to remember a person or event.
The Washington Monument honours George Washington, the first president.
Mount Rushmore has the faces of four presidents carved in stone.
check: Something built to remember a person or event
How many faces are on Mount Rushmore?
lessons.try: Look at a picture of Mount Rushmore and count the faces.

learn: Independence Day, July 4, celebrates when the country declared its independence in 1776.
Thanksgiving is a day to give thanks. Veterans Day honours people who served in the military.
Presidents' Day honours presidents. Martin Luther King Jr. Day honours a leader who worked for fairness.
check: People who served in the military
Martin Luther King Jr. worked for...
lessons.try: Pick a holiday and tell why it is celebrated.
